title: Routing, Feature Folders, and Tests
summary: Map URLs to pages with React Router 8, load data before render, organize code by feature behind public APIs, and test like a user with Testing Library.
intro: A real app has many pages, many features, and many people changing it at once. React Router maps each URL to its page and loads the page's data before it renders. A layout by feature keeps each part of the app in one folder behind a public API. And tests written with Testing Library prove, on every change, that the app still works the way a user uses it.

steps.title: Routes, layouts, and loaders
steps.body:
React Router 8 in data mode describes routes as objects. You create the router once, outside React, with `createBrowserRouter(routes)`, and render it with `<RouterProvider router={router} />`. A route has a `path` and a `Component`. Child routes render inside their parent's `<Outlet>`, so a layout route draws the shell once for every page under it, and an `index` route is the page at the parent's own path.

`:projectId` in a path is a URL param, read with `useParams()`. Params are always strings, so parse and validate them. Link with `<Link to>`, or `<NavLink>`, which marks the current page with `aria-current="page"`.

A `loader` runs as soon as a navigation starts, before the page renders. With TanStack Query it calls `ensureQueryData`, so the page's `useQuery` finds its data already cached. A `middleware` runs before the loaders, which is where Taskboard checks the session. And what a link should restore, like filters and the page number, belongs in the URL's search params, not in state.

examples.title: The route tree
examples.prompt: Read the app's routes: which URL renders which page, what runs first, and what shows when something fails.
examples.code:
export const routes: RouteObject[] = [
  { path: "/login", Component: LoginPage, ErrorBoundary: RouteError },
  {
    id: "root",
    path: "/",
    middleware: [authMiddleware],
    // The user authMiddleware loaded. Having a loader also makes the middleware run on the first page load.
    loader: ({ context }) => context.get(userContext),
    Component: RootLayout,
    HydrateFallback: AppLoading,
    ErrorBoundary: RouteError,
    children: [
      { index: true, loader: () => redirect("/projects") },
      { path: "projects", Component: ProjectsPage, ErrorBoundary: RouteError },
      {
        path: "projects/:projectId",
        loader: projectLoader,
        Component: ProjectLayout,
        ErrorBoundary: RouteError,
        children: [
          { index: true, Component: TaskBoard, action: quickAddAction },
          { path: "list", Component: TaskList },
          { path: "members", Component: MembersPage },
          { path: "stats", Component: ProjectStatsTab },
        ],
      },
      { path: "tasks/:taskId", loader: taskLoader, Component: TaskDetailPage, ErrorBoundary: RouteError },
      { path: "tasks/:taskId/edit", loader: taskLoader, Component: EditTaskPage, ErrorBoundary: RouteError },
      { path: "tasks/:taskId/delete", action: deleteTaskAction },
      { path: "team", Component: UserDirectory, ErrorBoundary: RouteError },
      // ...
      { path: "*", Component: NotFound },
    ],
  },
];
examples.explanation: `/login` is public. Every other page sits under the root route, whose `middleware` runs `authMiddleware` first: an anonymous visitor is redirected to `/login?next=` plus the page they wanted. The root's `Component` is the shell, and its `<Outlet>` shows the matched child. `projects/:projectId` is a layout too: the project's name and tabs, with the board as its `index` route and the list, members, and stats as children. Each page route has an `ErrorBoundary`, so a missing project or a crash shows an error page inside the shell, not a blank screen. The `*` route catches every other URL. The settings routes, in the elided lines, use `lazy`, so their code downloads on the first visit only.

examples.title: Loading before render
examples.prompt: Read the loader of `/projects/:projectId`, which runs before the project's page renders.
examples.explanation: The param arrives as a string, so the loader parses it and answers 404 for anything that isn't a positive whole number. It reads the app's `QueryClient` from the router context and calls `ensureQueryData` for the project and for the board's first page, in parallel with `Promise.all`. `ensureQueryData` returns cached data at once, or fetches it and caches it. When the page renders, its `useQuery` calls find both in the cache, so there's no spinner and no waterfall where the board waits for the project. Throwing `data(..., { status: 404 })` hands the 404 to the route's `ErrorBoundary`. The loader returns `null`, because the cache, not the loader, holds the data.

examples.title: Filters in the URL
examples.prompt: Read `useTaskFilters`, which keeps the board's and the list's filters in the URL's search params.
examples.explanation: `useSearchParams` reads and writes the query string the way `useState` reads and writes state, but the value lives in the URL. So a filtered board survives a reload, can be shared as a link, and the back button undoes a filter. `parseTaskFilters` turns the strings into typed filters and ignores values that make no sense, because anyone can type a URL. `setFilter` builds the next params from the current ones, leaves out values at their default so URLs stay short, and goes back to page 1. `replace: true` is for the search box: typing changes the URL without adding a history entry per letter.

steps.title: Feature folders and boundaries
steps.body:
Group code by feature, not by kind. Everything about tasks, its components, hooks, requests, types, and tests, lives in `src/features/tasks/`, so a change to tasks happens in one folder, and removing a feature means removing a folder. Code that belongs to no feature lives in shared folders: primitives like `Button` and `Field` in `components/ui`, general hooks in `hooks`, and the API client, the clock, and formatting in `lib`. The `app` folder only wires things together: the routes, the providers, and the shell.

Each feature has a public API, its `index.ts`. Other code imports from `@/features/tasks`, never from a file inside it, so a feature can reorganize its own files without breaking anyone, and a lint rule enforces that boundary.

Each layer has one job, so you always know where a change goes. A component draws and handles events, a hook decides what happens, the feature's `api.ts` describes requests and cache keys, and `lib/api-client.ts` speaks HTTP.

examples.title: The map
examples.prompt: Read the map of `src/` from the README, the first file to open in a codebase you just joined.
examples.code:
src/
  main.tsx              the entry: providers around the router, inside <StrictMode>
  app/                  wiring: the routes, the router, the providers, the shell, error pages
  components/ui/        primitives every feature uses: Button, Field, Dialog, Menu, Tag, Avatar, ...
  components/layout/    the shell's parts: Sidebar, Header, SearchBox, ThemeToggle
  features/
    auth/               login, logout, the session, the middleware that guards routes
    projects/           the projects page, a project's layout and tabs, rename, stats, members
    tasks/              the board, the list, a task's page, editing, and every task mutation
    comments/           a task's comments: pages of 10, posting with useOptimistic
    users/              the Team page
    watchers/           who watches a task: a small, finished feature to copy
    labels/             label chips, the label picker, the label filter
    settings/           theme and density, and the admin-only danger zone (a lazy route)
  hooks/                hooks with no feature: localStorage, media queries, debouncing, theme
  lib/                  the API client, the clock, formatting, storage, the cache keys
  styles/               design tokens and the global reset
  test/                 the test setup, the fake API (MSW), its fixtures, and render helpers
api/                    the mock API (Express): server.ts, then routes/, auth, storage, views
e2e/                    Playwright specs
public/                 files served as they are: the favicon and the avatars
examples.explanation: Follow one action through the layers: dragging a card to Done. `BoardColumn`, in `features/tasks/components`, handles the drop and calls `useTransitionTask` from `features/tasks/hooks`. The hook moves the card in the cache at once and calls `transitionTask` from the feature's `api.ts`. That calls `apiFetch` in `lib/api-client.ts`, which sends `POST /v1/tasks/3/transition`. Vite's dev server forwards `/v1` to the mock API in `api/`, which checks the session and the user's role, saves, and answers with the task. Back in the hook, the cache gets the server's copy and the board refreshes. The README traces this same journey, file by file.

examples.title: A feature's public API
examples.prompt: Read what the tasks feature lets the rest of the app import.
examples.explanation: The routes need the pages, the loaders, and the actions, the header's search box needs `useTaskFilters`, and other features need the types and labels, so those are exported. Everything else, like `TaskCard`, `BoardColumn`, and the mutation hooks, stays private to the feature. `api.ts` and `cache.ts` may also be imported directly, because they depend only on `lib/`. That's how `ProjectCard` prefetches the board without pulling task components into the projects feature. `type Task` marks a type-only export, which the build erases.

examples.title: The boundary rule
examples.prompt: Read the lint rule that keeps features from reaching into each other's files.
examples.explanation: An import of `@/features/tasks/components/TaskCard` from anywhere fails `npm run lint` with the message in the rule, and the Problems panel shows it as soon as you save. Inside a feature, files import each other with relative paths like `./TaskCard`, which the patterns don't match, so the rule only guards the boundary. Teams write rules like this because a folder convention that nothing checks erodes one shortcut at a time.

steps.title: Testing like a user
steps.body:
Component tests render into jsdom, a browser page simulated in Node, and Vitest runs them. Testing Library finds elements the way a user does: by role and accessible name, like `getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })`, then by label and by text. `getBy` throws when nothing matches, `queryBy` returns `null` to prove something is absent, and `findBy` waits for something that appears later. After `userEvent.setup()`, `await user.click(...)` and `await user.type(...)` fire the full sequence of events a person would. jest-dom adds matchers like `toBeInTheDocument`, `toHaveValue`, and `toHaveFocus`.

Test what the screen shows and what the server receives, never state or which hooks ran, so a refactor that keeps the behavior keeps the tests green. Taskboard's test helpers in `src/test/render.tsx` render with the same providers as the app, a fresh `QueryClient` per test, and a memory router, and MSW answers requests from a fake API in memory. A request that no handler expects fails the test, and so does any `console.error`.

examples.title: A component test
examples.prompt: Read three of `TaskCard`'s tests, then run the whole file with `npm run test:run -- --reporter=verbose src/features/tasks/task-card.test.tsx`.

examples.explanation: `renderCard` builds a real task from the fixtures, the same rows as the API's seed, and renders the card as a logged-in user. Each test reads like a sentence about behavior, and Vitest prints those sentences, so a failure says what broke. The link is found by its role and its visible name, so the test also proves the link is accessible. The overdue label depends on the date, and `vite.config.ts` fixes the app's clock at 2026-10-01 in tests, so the test never breaks on a different day. The Escape test drives the keyboard like a person and checks where focus lands. Run tests through `npm run`, which adds the `--configLoader native` flag this workspace needs, and `--reporter=verbose` lists every test by name. The timings vary from run to run.

examples.title: Faking a failure
examples.prompt: Read two tests of the Team page: the list loads, and a server error offers a Retry that works.
examples.explanation: `renderWithProviders` renders the page as Ada, inside the app's providers. The fake API answers `GET /v1/users` from the seed data, so the first test only waits: `findByText` retries until Ada appears, or fails after a timeout. The second test changes one answer with `server.use`: the next request to `/v1/users` gets a 500 problem, once, and every later request works again. The test then does what a user would: it sees the alert, clicks Retry, and sees the list. It never looks at `isError` or `refetch`, so it keeps passing however the component is written, as long as it behaves.

examples.title: Testing a redirect
examples.prompt: Read the test that proves an anonymous visitor is sent to the login page.
examples.explanation: `renderApp` renders the real route tree in a memory router, middleware and loaders included, here as nobody, so the fake API answers `/v1/me` with a 401. The test starts at `/projects/1` and checks where the user ends up: the login heading on screen, and the router's location, with the page they wanted in `next`, URL-encoded. One short test covers the route config, the middleware, the redirect, and the login page together, the way a user meets them.

recap:
- Create the router once with `createBrowserRouter`, nest pages in layout routes that render an `<Outlet>`, and parse params, which are always strings.
- Load a page's data in its route loader with `ensureQueryData`, guard routes with middleware, and keep filters in search params.
- Group code by feature behind an `index.ts`, keep shared code in `components/ui`, `hooks`, and `lib`, and enforce the boundary with a lint rule.
- Test like a user: find elements by role and label, act with user-event, fake the network with MSW, and assert what the screen shows.
